raw_case_text:
A 41-year-old male patient with lymphoma had previously visited a local hospital and underwent bronchoscopy to examine the BALF. The routine microbiological examination did not detect any pathogenic bacteria; Gram staining did not show any bacteria; the culture did not show fungal growth; Grocott's methenamine (hexamine) silver technique did not show PJP cysts, and tuberculosis smears did not detect acid-fast bacteria. However, BALF-NGS found 5225 PJP reads and four Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) reads. Due to the uncertainty regarding tuberculosis infection, he was transferred to our designated tuberculosis hospital for continued treatment.
The patient presented with relapsed refractory diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (R/RDLBCL) with MYC, BCL-2, and BCL-6 expression. After treatment with R-CHOP (rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone), R-GDP (rituximab, cisplatin, gemcitabine, and dexamethasone), venetoclax, obutinib, and immune checkpoint inhibitors were administered. The patient developed acute type 1 respiratory failure, severe pneumonia, PJP, cytomegalovirus retinitis, secondary immune deficiency, and secondary pulmonary tuberculosis.
The patient underwent a computed tomography (CT) examination after admission (Figure 1A), which indicated that two lung infections should be considered first. In addition, the immune response to MTB by T-cell receptor clustering was negative, and MTB complex from sputum samples, non-tuberculous mycobacterial DNA, and tuberculosis DNA and RNA were negative. Meropenem (1 g q8h) was administered for infection, TMP-SMX 1.44 g q6h for PJP, and rifampicin, isoniazid, and levofloxacin for tuberculosis. Simultaneously, methylprednisolone 40 mg q12h was administered to control inflammation. Ganciclovir was used as a prophylactic treatment for cytomegalovirus retinitis, and tiopronin was used for liver protection.
Unfortunately, the patient developed drug-induced liver injury after six days of treatment, with alanine transaminase (ALT) levels up to 269 U/L and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) levels up to 299 U/L. Due to the gastrointestinal reaction of nausea and vomiting combined with drug-induced liver injury, the patient could not tolerate high-intensity treatment, so the dose of TMP-SMX was reduced to 0.96 g q8h, combined with micafungin 0.2 g qd for PJP treatment. However, after four days of continued treatment, a reexamination CT scan indicated the progression of the infection (Figure 1B). The patient's high fever remained unrelieved, with a temperature as high as 40.4 C (see Figure 2 for the temperature trend chart) accompanied by shortness of breath and chest tightness. Blood gas analysis indicated type 2 respiratory failure and the arterial oxygen tension (PaO2) decreased to 57 mmHg. Indicators of particularly abnormal laboratory tests, including levels of procalcitonin (PCT) 5.32 ng/mL, C-reactive protein (CRP) 167.53 mg/L, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) 564 U/L, and white blood cell (WBC) count 2.7*109/L, are shown in Table 1. 
Based on the persistent fever, tachypnoea, PaO2 of 57 mmHg, arterial oxygen saturation (SaO2) of 89% at rest, and extensive interstitial shadowing on chest CT, the patient was classified as having severe PJP according to the PJP grade. Therefore, the treatment regimen for PJP was adjusted to TMP-SMX 0.96 g q6h + caspofungin 50 mg qd, while teicoplanin 0.4 g q12h was added to enhance the anti-infection effect.
After a multidisciplinary team discussion, the anti-tuberculosis drugs were discontinued because MTB was considered a non-pathogenic bacterium. Leukocyte and platelet-ascending drugs were used, human immunoglobulin was added, and nutrition was improved.
After four days of treatment for multiple infections, the patient's temperature decreased to 37 C, and acute infection indicators improved (PCT 0.39 ng/mL, CRP 30.30 mg/L). Anti-infection de-escalation therapy consisted of cefoperazone and sulbactam 3 g q8h. PJP treatment continued for 30 days, and pulmonary infection lesions were completely relieved (Figure 1C). TMP-SMX 0.96 g qd was continuously administered as a PJP prophylactic therapy. The patient then began treatment for the lymphoma.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 41-year-old male with relapsed/refractory triple-hit diffuse large B-cell lymphoma was transferred for severe pneumonia, acute type I respiratory failure, and co-detection of Pneumocystis jirovecii and Mycobacterium tuberculosis on bronchoalveolar lavage sequencing.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient had relapsed/refractory diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (R/R DLBCL) with MYC, BCL-2, and BCL-6 expression treated sequentially with R-CHOP, R-GDP, venetoclax, orelabrutinib (obutinib), and immune checkpoint inhibitors. He developed severe pneumonia, acute type I respiratory failure, cytomegalovirus retinitis, and secondary immunodeficiency. At a local hospital, bronchoscopy with BALF routine microbiology, Gram stain, fungal culture, Grocott's methenamine silver (GMS) stain, and AFB smears were all negative, but BALF next-generation sequencing (NGS) detected 5,225 Pneumocystis jirovecii reads and 4 Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) reads, prompting transfer to a designated tuberculosis hospital.
subjective.past_medical_history: Relapsed/refractory diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (MYC/BCL-2/BCL-6 positive) treated with R-CHOP, R-GDP, venetoclax, obutinib, and immune checkpoint inhibitors; cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis; secondary immunodeficiency.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for severe dyspnea/acute respiratory failure; subsequently developed nausea, vomiting, persistent high fever up to 40.4 °C, shortness of breath, and chest tightness during hospitalization.

objective.physical_examination: During hospital progression (day 10): High fever up to 40.4 °C, tachypnea, shortness of breath, and resting arterial oxygen saturation (SaO2) 89%.
objective.routine_investigations: Local hospital routine BALF workup: Negative bacterial culture, Gram stain, fungal culture, GMS stain, and AFB smear. Admission tuberculosis workup at referral hospital: Negative MTB T-cell receptor clustering immune assay, negative sputum MTB complex, negative nontuberculous mycobacterial DNA, and negative TB DNA and RNA. Day 6 drug-induced liver injury labs: ALT elevated to 269 U/L and AST elevated to 299 U/L. Day 10 clinical deterioration labs: Type 2 respiratory failure with PaO2 57 mmHg and SaO2 89%, WBC 2.7 x 10^9/L, procalcitonin (PCT) 5.32 ng/mL, C-reactive protein (CRP) 167.53 mg/L, and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) 564 U/L.
objective.advanced_workup: Pre-transfer local hospital BALF mNGS: 5,225 sequence reads of Pneumocystis jirovecii and 4 sequence reads of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB). Admission and serial chest CT scans: Extensive bilateral pulmonary interstitial shadowing and infectious infiltrates that initially progressed on day 10 after TMP-SMX dose reduction and completely resolved after 30 days of combination therapy.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Severe Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP; confirmed by 5,225 reads on BALF mNGS, LDH 564 U/L, PaO2 57 mmHg, and extensive bilateral interstitial infiltrates on CT) complicated by anti-TB/TMP-SMX drug-induced liver injury in a patient with relapsed/refractory DLBCL; active pulmonary tuberculosis was ruled out by multidisciplinary review and negative confirmatory MTB molecular/immunological assays (4 BALF reads deemed non-pathogenic colonization/background). Plan and clinical course: Initially treated with TMP-SMX (1.44 g q6h), meropenem (1 g q8h), rifampicin, isoniazid, levofloxacin, methylprednisolone (40 mg q12h), prophylactic ganciclovir (for CMV retinitis), and tiopronin. On day 6, nausea/vomiting and hepatotoxicity (ALT 269 U/L, AST 299 U/L) prompted reducing TMP-SMX to 0.96 g q8h plus micafungin (0.2 g qd), which led to clinical and CT progression by day 10 (fever 40.4 °C, PaO2 57 mmHg, PCT 5.32 ng/mL, CRP 167.53 mg/L). Following multidisciplinary consultation, anti-TB drugs were discontinued, and treatment was intensified to TMP-SMX (0.96 g q6h) combined with caspofungin (50 mg qd), teicoplanin (0.4 g q12h), IVIG, and hematopoietic growth factors. Within 4 days, his fever resolved (37 °C) and inflammatory markers dropped (PCT 0.39 ng/mL, CRP 30.30 mg/L), allowing de-escalation of antibacterial therapy to cefoperazone-sulbactam (3 g q8h). He completed 30 days of PJP treatment with complete CT resolution, transitioned to prophylactic TMP-SMX (0.96 g qd), and resumed lymphoma therapy.
